title: Fuel Duty Freeze Extended as Iran War Drives Up Prices; Critics Call It a U-Turn
summary: Drivers can breathe a small sigh of relief — for now. Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced Wednesday that the 5-pence-per-litre cut on fuel duty, first introduced in 2022, will be extended until the end of 2026, scrapping plans to phase it out in September. The decision comes as petrol prices hit their highest since the start of the US-Israel war in Iran, reaching an average of 158.52p per litre on Monday, according to the RAC. "We're backing drivers by extending the freeze on fuel duty," Starmer told the House of Commons, pointing to turmoil in the Middle East that has disrupted global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies. The fuel duty cut was originally a temporary measure by the Conservative government after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent prices soaring. It has been extended multiple times since. In addition, Starmer announced a cut of over one-third on red diesel duty — to 6.48p per litre — from mid-next month until year-end, aimed at helping farmers who use it in agricultural machinery. There will also be a 12-month holiday on vehicle excise duty for heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) to ease supply chain costs that can drive up consumer prices. But the move drew sharp political fire. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch thanked Starmer for what she called a "U-turn," noting her party had demanded the freeze in March. Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride claimed Labour was "forced into a U-turn" and that its planned tax hike would have "hammered hardworking families." The RAC's head of policy, Simon Williams, welcomed the extension but warned of uncertainty ahead: "Will drivers be hit with the full 5p in one go in the spring, will a new phasing be agreed, or will the government even abandon an increase altogether?" For now, the freeze offers a buffer against volatile global energy markets. But with geopolitical tensions showing no sign of easing, the question of what happens next year looms large for every motorist.
why_it_matters: The fuel duty freeze illustrates how wars and political tensions thousands of miles away trickle down to everyday costs, directly affecting how much a teenager’s family pays for fuel and, as a result, the price of food and other goods that travel by truck.

background_read: Keir Starmer has been the UK’s Prime Minister since July 2024, leading a Labour government. Fuel duty is a major tax that the British government has often frozen or cut for political reasons, especially when global oil prices spike.

The original 5p-per-litre cut was introduced in March 2022 by the Conservative government after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent oil and gas prices soaring. Since then, it has been extended multiple times, making it one of the longest-running temporary fuel tax reductions.

Now the US-Israel war in Iran has further disrupted oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, driving up prices at the pump. The RAC (Royal Automobile Club, a motorists’ organisation) tracks fuel prices and campaigns on behalf of drivers.

Kemi Badenoch, the current leader of the Conservative Party, accused Labour of a ‘U-turn’ because the government had previously signalled it would phase out the cut in September 2025. Shadow Chancellor Mel Stride (the opposition’s shadow finance minister) claimed Labour had been ‘forced into a U-turn’ by Conservative pressure.

Red diesel is a lower-taxed fuel used mainly by farmers and construction, and heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) are large trucks that carry goods. By cutting red diesel duty and offering a 12-month holiday on vehicle excise duty for HGVs, the government aims to shield food prices and supply chains from rising transport costs.

└─ specific: Petrol prices hit a record 158.52p per litre on Monday, the highest since the US-Israel war in Iran began.
CONTEXT: The 5p cut was a temporary Conservative measure from 2022, after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sent prices surging. It has been extended several times since.

ADDITIONAL MEASURES: Starmer also announced a cut of over one-third on red diesel duty for farmers, and a 12-month vehicle excise duty holiday for heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) to ease supply chain costs.

POLITICAL REACTION: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called it a ‘U-turn,’ noting her party had demanded the freeze in March. Shadow Chancellor Mel Stride said Labour had been ‘forced into a U-turn’ and that the previous planned tax hike would have ‘hammered’ families.
INDUSTRY WARNING: The RAC’s Simon Williams welcomed the extension but warned of uncertainty: will drivers face the full 5p increase later, a phased return, or even permanent abolition?
LOOKING AHEAD: With geopolitical tensions showing no sign of easing, the question of what happens after the freeze looms large for every motorist.

perspectives.description: Extending the cut shields households and farmers from immediate price shocks at a time when global oil markets are unstable. The extra red diesel reduction and HGV tax break help keep food production and supply chains running smoothly.

Repeated fuel duty freezes reduce government revenue that could be spent on public services or green transition. Critics also argue that subsidising fossil fuels delays the move to cleaner transport and undermines climate goals.

Fuel duty policy in the UK has long been driven by short-term political reactions to price spikes rather than a long-term strategy. Governments of both main parties have frozen or cut duty for over a decade, creating uncertainty and making tax revenue reliant on volatile oil prices.

Future governments may need to design a more stable system that adjusts fuel taxes gradually, perhaps linking them to carbon emissions while offering targeted support. If geopolitical tensions persist, the question of how to fund roads and public transport without fuel duty will become more urgent.
